They say that when the world was young and still uncapped, there was no sun, only a golden bird asleep beneath the sea. Sometimes it stirred, and a little brightness escaped between its feathers. This was why the fish had silver eyes, and why the rivers climbed their banks at night: they were trying to carry that brightness home.

In those days a lantern-maker named Tom lived at the foot of Sun Mountain. His lanterns were beautifully made, with doors of hammered tin and handles shaped like vines, but there was nothing to put inside them. People bought them anyway, hoping.

One night, while Tom sat beside his cold hearth, a feather came floating upstream.

He caught it in an empty lantern. Its glow showed him every crack in his walls, every worn place in his hands. Then it shone brighter, and through the open doorway he saw his neighbours stumbling from their houses, covering their eyes.

Tom closed the lantern door.

From outside came a voice like stones shifting underwater.

“Who has shut away my feather?”

A golden bird stood in the river. Water streamed from its wings, climbing into the darkness.

“I have,” said Tom. “It hurts us to look at it.”

“Then you are not ready for light.”

“We might be,” Tom said, “if there were a little less of it.”

The bird lowered its great head to his doorway. Tom could feel the heat of its breath through the tin.

“Blow on the feather,” it said.

Tom opened the door a finger’s width and blew. A spark broke loose and settled on his hearth. He blew again, and another lodged in the wick of his lantern. Soon there were small flames all through the village, each one bright enough to see by and gentle enough to approach.

For seven nights the bird stayed with them. It taught the children to carry embers in clay bowls and the old people to bank a fire beneath ash. Tom learned to fit shutters to his lanterns. His neighbours learned that light could be shared without the first flame growing smaller.

On the eighth night, the bird climbed Sun Mountain. At the summit it spread its wings, and morning entered Hollowmere.

Tom’s hair had turned white by then. He lived long enough to forget the names of several kings, but never forgot how to catch a spark. Each winter, people gathered at his door to watch him toss an ember from one bare hand to the other.

And still the rivers run uphill at night. They have carried the bird’s brightness through the world all day; in the dark, they go looking for its nest.
